--- title: Web scraping with Beautiful Soup author: Marie-Hélène Burle --- :::{.def} The internet is a trove of information. A lot of it is publicly available and thus suitable for use in research. Extracting that information and putting it in an organized format for analysis can however be extremely tedious. Web scraping tools allow to automate parts of that process and Python is a popular language for the task. In this workshop, I will guide you through an example using the package [Beautiful Soup](https://beautiful-soup-4.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). ::: ## HTML and CSS [HyperText Markup Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML) (HTML) is the standard markup language for websites: it encodes the information related to the formatting and structure of webpages. Additionally, some of the customization can be stored in [Cascading Style Sheets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSS) (CSS) files. HTML uses tags of the form: ```{.html} Your content ``` Some tags have attributes: ```{.html} Your content ``` :::{.example} Examples: ::: Site structure: - `

This is a heading of level 2

` - `

This is a paragraph

` Formatting: - `This is bold` - `This is the text for a link` ## Web scrapping Web scraping is a general term for a set of tools which allow for the extraction of data from the web automatically. While most of the data on the internet is publicly available, it is illegal to scrape some sites and you should always look into the policy of a site before attempting to scrape it. Some sites will also block you if you submit too many requests in a short amount of time, so remember to scrape responsibly by doing the following: - Look for a public API for the site. If there is an API, use it instead of scraping (it will be a lot easier). - Add `robots.txt` at the end of the URL of a site to see whether it says anything about scraping. - Add some delay with `time.sleep` between requests. - Google whether or not the site you are interested in can be scraped. - Look for information on the site itself. ## Example for this workshop We will use the [Theoi project](https://www.theoi.com/). Our goal is to get a DataFrame with the name of the Greek gods as a variable and their parents as a 2nd variable. :::{.note} Theoi is the ancient Greek word for "gods". ::: ## Install packages For this section, you need to install the following packages in a virtual environment (you can create a new one or activate the one you used in the previous days): - `requests` - `beautifulsoup4` - `polars` This is why we need these packages: | Package | Usage | |--|--| | [requests](https://github.com/psf/requests) | Allows you to send commands to a web server. In our case, we use it to get the HTML of the page we are interested in. | | [beautifulsoup4](https://www.crummy.com/software/BeautifulSoup/bs4/doc/) | Makes it easy to pull data out of HTML files. | | [polars](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars) | The DataFrame library that we will use to store our data. | : {tbl-colwidths="[20, 80]"} ## Explore the site carefully The first step is to get familiar with the site. You want to understand its structure, what data it contains, and how that data is organized. Of course, you also want to think carefully about what data you want and be clear about what your goals are before you start coding. In our case, we should start from [the page of the Greek gods](https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/greek-gods.html). From it, we want a list of all the URLs of the subcategories of Greek gods (e.g. [Olypian gods](https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/olympian-gods.html), [Titan gods](https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/titans.html), etc.). Then, from each of those sub-pages, we want the URLs of individual gods (e.g. [Aphrodite](https://www.theoi.com/Olympios/Aphrodite.html), [Apollo](https://www.theoi.com/Olympios/Apollon.html), etc.). Finally, from those pages, we want the names of the parents. ## Load packages Let's load the packages that will make scraping websites with Python easier: ::: {#a7bd0c59 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # External packages: import requests # To download the HTML data from a site from bs4 import BeautifulSoup # To parse the HTML data import polars as pl # To store the data # Modules from the standard library: import time # To add a delay between each requests import re # To use regular expressions ``` ::: ## Send request to the main site Let's create a string with the main URL we want to scrape: ::: {#62ba8291 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage_url = "https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/greek-gods.html" ``` ::: First, we send a request to that URL and save the response in a variable called `r`: ::: {#311f5541 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} r = requests.get(mainpage_url) ``` ::: Let's see what our response looks like: ::: {#625c3ab6 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} r ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ``` ::: ::: ::: {#38ddd4ad .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} r.status_code ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 200 ``` ::: ::: If you look in the [list of HTTP status codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_HTTP_status_codes), you can see that a response with a code of `200` means that the request was successful. ## Explore the raw data To get the actual content of the response as unicode (text), we can use the `text` property of the response. This will give us the raw HTML markup from the webpage. Let's print the first 800 characters: ::: {#b76ef01f .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(r.text[:800]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Greek Gods & Goddesses | Theoi Greek Mythology Greek Gods & Goddesses | Theoi Greek Mythology Greek Gods & Goddesses | Theoi Greek Mythology ``` ::: ::: - using `select_one()` which accepts CSS selectors: ::: {#a253d2c3 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage.select_one("title") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` Greek Gods & Goddesses | Theoi Greek Mythology ``` ::: ::: If you use these methods on elements that occur multiple times, they will return the first element: ::: {#2c223164 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage.a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` Theoi Project - Greek Mythology ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b0969a99 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage.find("a") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` Theoi Project - Greek Mythology ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4fe8055f .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage.select_one("a") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` Theoi Project - Greek Mythology ``` ::: ::: If you want to extract all elements, you need to use instead: - `find_all()` for HTML markers ::: {#619fe625 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage.find_all("a")[:5] # let's only print the first 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` [Theoi Project - Greek Mythology, HOME, OLYMPIANS, Aphrodite, Apollo] ``` ::: ::: - `select()` for CSS selectors: ::: {#e4a64508 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage.select("a")[:5] # let's only print the first 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` [Theoi Project - Greek Mythology, HOME, OLYMPIANS, Aphrodite, Apollo] ``` ::: ::: Both methods return a BeautifulSoup `ResultSet` object which behaves like a list. :::{.info} **Difference between methods:** | | Python objects | CSS selectors | |--------------|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------| | Single match | `find()` | `select_one()` | | All matches | `find_all()` | `select()` | | Dependency | None | [Soup Sieve](https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve) | | Performance | Faster | Slower due to CSS parsing | ::: ## Identify relevant markers The HTML code for this webpage contains the data we are interested in, but it is mixed in with a lot of HTML formatting and data we don't care about. We need to extract the data relevant to us and turn it into a workable format. The first step is to find the HTML markers that contain our data. One option is to use a web inspector or—even easier—the [SelectorGadget](https://selectorgadget.com/), a JavaScript bookmarklet built by [Andrew Cantino](https://andrewcantino.com/). To use this tool, go to the [SelectorGadget](https://selectorgadget.com/) website and drag the link of the bookmarklet to your bookmarks bar. Now, go to [the Greek gods page](https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/greek-gods.html) and click on the bookmarklet in your bookmarks bar. You will see a floating box at the bottom of your screen. As you move your mouse across the screen, an orange rectangle appears around each element over which you pass and it give you the HTML tag of that element. Your goal is to select the HTML marker that matches the elements you want and only those by first clicking on one element of interest to select all similar elements, then, in a second step (when the box is red), to click on one selected element that you don't want to remove those. What we want in our example are hyperlinks (since we first need the list of sub-pages for the sub-categories of Greek gods). Hyperlinks in HTML are marked by the `a` tag. So as you move the orange box over various elements, make sure to click when you see `a` in the bottom left corner of the box. If you hover over one of the images and see `a img`, you might think that you are on the right track, but if you actually select it by clicking on it, the selected tag in the box is `img`. Meaning no hyperlink, so that's not good (you can click [Clear]{.codelike} to clear the selection and start again). Now, if you hover over one of the captions below the images, you can see `h3 a` in the bottom corner of the orange box and if you click on it, the tag is `a`. So that's good. But that has selected all the hyperlinks in the page and of course we only want the links that leads to the sub-categories of gods. So click on links you don't want to deselect their different types until you only have the links you want. In the end, the tag you want is called `.caption a` and there should be 11 of them in the page. :::{.note} To close the gadget, click on the cross in the right of the box. ::: ## Get the sub-categories URLs Now we can use `select` with the CSS selector `.caption a` to extract the URLs of the sub-categories of gods: ::: {#e235fa33 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage_captions = mainpage.select(".caption a") ``` ::: Let's first prototype our code on the first link: ::: {#33cebc00 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage_captions[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` OLYMPIAN GODS ``` ::: ::: This gives you the full hyperlink code. What you want out of it is the URL. You extract it with: ::: {#e284034a .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} mainpage_captions[0].get("href") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` 'olympian-gods.html' ``` ::: ::: Unfortunately, this is not a full URL and you need to prepend `https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/` to it. This string is actually the base URL that you will have to prepend everywhere, so let's create a variable with it: ::: {#7c3cbe1d .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} base_url = "https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/" ``` ::: We can now concatenate it with our code to get the full URL: ::: {#91cd6e6f .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} base_url + mainpage_captions[0].get("href") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/olympian-gods.html' ``` ::: ::: That looks good! We got the first URL. :::{.exo} :::{.yourturn} Your turn: ::: How would you get the second URL? ::: Of course, we need to do this on all the elements of `captions`. For this we use a for loop. First, we create an empty list that we will fill with the URLs as the loop runs: ::: {#c0a52def .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} subcats_urls = [] ``` ::: Now we run the loop and fill in our empty list with `append`: ::: {#be57ee60 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} for caption in mainpage_captions: subcats_urls.append(base_url + caption.get("href")) ``` ::: :::{.exo} :::{.yourturn} Your turn: ::: Print the last 3 URLs. ::: ## Get the gods URLs Now, for each sub-category of gods, we want the URLs of all the gods pages. The methodology is exactly the same as what we did previously. Let's do it for the first subcategory at the URL . First, we need to index that first URL from our list `subcats_urls`: ::: {#15d246ac .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} subcats_url0 = subcats_urls[0] subcats_url0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/olympian-gods.html' ``` ::: ::: Then we send a request to that URL: ::: {#33b68d55 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} r = requests.get(subcats_url0) ``` ::: Now we turn it into soup: ::: {#57e5b66d .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} subcat0 = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser") ``` ::: You can play with the SelectorGadget to double-check that the HTML tag is the same, then you can use it to extract all the caption with the links to the gods pages: ::: {#d6240632 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} subcat0_captions = subcat0.select(".caption a") ``` ::: Let's print the first element to make sure it looks like what we expect: ::: {#5a2d4bad .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} subcat0_captions[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` APHRODITE ``` ::: ::: Let's extract the URL part of the hyperlink: ::: {#858fa837 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} subcat0_captions[0].get("href") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` '../Olympios/Aphrodite.html' ``` ::: ::: Now, to recreate the actual URL, you prepend `base_url` as we did before: ::: {#4a5ac29d .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} base_url + subcat0_captions[0].get("href") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Aphrodite.html' ``` ::: ::: :::{.notenoit} This URL might look peculiar to you but it is actually totally valid: \ `..` represents the parent directory and \ `https://www.theoi.com/Olympios/../Olympios/Aphrodite.html` is actually exactly the same as \ `https://www.theoi.com/Olympios/Aphrodite.html`. ::: Now that we checked that the code works on a single entry, we can do it on all elements of the ResultSet: ::: {#571c09fb .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls0 = [] for caption in subcat0_captions: gods_urls0.append(base_url + caption.get("href")) ``` ::: As a sanity check, let's see how many gods URL we have for this first subcategory of gods: ::: {#b20d799c .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} len(gods_urls0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ``` 27 ``` ::: ::: If you go to the [Olympian gods page](https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/olympian-gods.html), you will see that there are indeed 27 gods in that category, so we are good. Let's print the first 5 URLs as a safety check: ::: {#e0f2be02 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls0[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ``` ['https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Aphrodite.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Apollon.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Ares.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Artemis.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Athena.html'] ``` ::: ::: It worked! 🙂 Now we need to do that for all the subcategories of gods in a big loop and we will then have the URLs for *all* the Greek gods. In addition to the code, we will add a little delay at each iteration so that the website we are scraping doesn't block us. It is considered good practice to not overwhelm the server by creating too much traffic at once: ::: {#91c018e2 .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls = [] for subcats_url in subcats_urls: r = requests.get(subcats_url) subcat = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser") subcat_captions = subcat.select(".caption a") for caption in subcat_captions: gods_urls.append(base_url + caption.get("href")) # Add a delay at each iteration time.sleep(0.1) ``` ::: :::{.note} Note the presence of a nested for loop (a for loop within a for loop). It is getting complicated! ::: Let's do a few sanity checks. First 5 URLs: ::: {#f1675c4a .cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=35} ``` ['https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Aphrodite.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Apollon.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Ares.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Artemis.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Olympios/Athena.html'] ``` ::: ::: Last 5: ::: {#9d7f9a87 .cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls[-5:] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=36} ``` ['https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Cult/HeraklesCult.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Cult/MousaiCult.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Cult/PanCult.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Cult/RheaCult.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Cult/TykheCult.html'] ``` ::: ::: Length of our list of gods URLs: ::: {#7dab948e .cell execution_count=38} ``` {.python .cell-code} len(gods_urls) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=37} ``` 174 ``` ::: ::: 5 URLs somewhere in the middle of the list: ::: {#fe29b5be .cell execution_count=39} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls[80:85] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=38} ``` ['https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Titan/TitanisTethys.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Protogenos/Thalassa.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Pontios/NereisThetis.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Pontios/Triton.html', 'https://www.theoi.com/greek-mythology/../Titan/Anemoi.html'] ``` ::: ::: ## Get the gods info Remember that our goal was to get the gods names and their parents names. As always, we test the code on a single element (here one god URL) first before we implement a loop. Let's extract the first gods URL from the list: ::: {#e22967fc .cell execution_count=40} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_urls0 = gods_urls[0] ``` ::: Now, we send a request and render as usual: ::: {#aa33d406 .cell execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code} r = requests.get(gods_urls0) god0 = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser") ``` ::: The first thing we need from this page is the name of the god (a goddess in this case). We should be able to do this from the title of this page. ::: {#ec591cd1 .cell execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code} god0.title ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=41} ``` APHRODITE - Greek Goddess of Love & Beauty (Roman Venus) ``` ::: ::: The title is in a `title` tag. To extract the text out of an HTML tag, you use the `get_text` method: ::: {#cac47cf2 .cell execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code} title0 = god0.title.get_text() title0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=42} ``` 'APHRODITE - Greek Goddess of Love & Beauty (Roman Venus)' ``` ::: ::: We then use a regular expression to clean the part of the title that we are not interested in: ::: {#b40eff9f .cell execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code} god_name0 = re.sub(r"\s*-.*$", "", title0) god_name0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=43} ``` 'APHRODITE' ``` ::: ::: :::{.note} Trick: LLMs are very good at writing regular expressions. Ask them to write them for you. Alternatively, if you want to learn regexp, [here](https://www.regular-expressions.info/quickstart.html) is an excellent site that explains them very nicely. ::: We could change the name from upper case to capitalized: ::: {#9b1502ee .cell execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code} god_name0.capitalize() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=44} ``` 'Aphrodite' ``` ::: ::: We now have the god's name which is the first thing we want for each god. The second thing we want is the names of the parents of that god. As we are now trying to extract a very type of element from the site, we have to go back to the SelectorGadget. This shows us that the element we need is under the HTML tag `tr:nth-child(1) td`. Let's extract that element: ::: {#2f4046a5 .cell execution_count=46} ``` {.python .cell-code} god0_parents = god0.select_one("tr:nth-child(1) td") god0_parents ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=45} ``` Zeus and Dione ``` ::: ::: Our element is in a `td` tag so we extract it with the `get_text` method: ::: {#0d5bd8ee .cell execution_count=47} ``` {.python .cell-code} god0_parents.get_text() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=46} ``` 'Zeus and Dione' ``` ::: ::: 🥳 We can now create a loop to run this code on all the elements of the ResultSet: ::: {#84e87399 .cell execution_count=48} ``` {.python .cell-code} gods_info = [] for god_url in gods_urls: r = requests.get(god_url) god = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser") title = god.title.get_text() god_name = re.sub(r"\s*-.*$", "", title).capitalize() god_parents = god.select_one("tr:nth-child(1) td").get_text() # Save the god name and its parents names in a tuple gods_info.append((god_name, god_parents)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}
